newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian export loss seen at $250 mln due to strike.
newsitem.headline: Indian export loss seen at $250 mln due to strike.

text.p: A 10-day strike by Indian truck owners caused a loss of at least $250 million in exports and left ports clogged with uncleared goods, exporters said on Friday.
"Our estimate of losses in exports due to the strike could be around $250 million," said Ramu Deora, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO).
Deora said the losses were mainly due to the cancellation of orders, especially of exports such as fruit and other perishables and seasonal items like summer fabrics.

Owners of nearly 2.2 million trucks ended the strike on Wednesday after the government agreed not to hold truckers responsible for collecting a five percent service tax and to hold off on a proposed rise in insurance premiums.
Deora said the strike delayed exports worth more than $1.0 billion and it would take at least 20 days to clear them.
"We are appealing to customs to clear export consignments during the weekend and holidays," he said.
Bombay port officials said trucks had started moving goods to and from the docks but did not specify how long it would it take to clear them.
S.P. Singh, a spokesman for the All-India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), said truck owners had lost about 36 billion rupees ($1 billion) due to the strike.
Analysts said the economy faced an estimated daily losses of about 70 billion to 80 billion rupees ($1.95 billion to $2.2 billion) a day.
They said the strike had severely affected the supply of raw materials to industrial units and pushed up fruit and vegetable prices by at least 25 percent.
"It is difficult to quantify the production losses," said FIEO's Deora.

The strike had disrupted the supply of essential commodities across the country and pushed up their prices. Worst affected were isolated north-eastern states, which depend largely on road transport for links with the rest of the country.
Traders said prices of sugar, oilseeds and oils, grains and pulses would remain firm for at least two to three days until fresh supplies began to arrive at marketplaces.
"The pipeline is still empty," said a trader.
Traders said an estimated 1,500 tonnes of imported non-ferrous metals, 2,500 tonnes of palm oil and 5,000 tonnes of sunflower oil awaited clearance.
